query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 1 wt% Y to Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance without sacrificing mechanical performance by forming a protective Y2O3 layer, resulting in a 30% reduction in oxidation rate at 1000 °C in air, while maintaining a room-temperature tensile ductility of 8-16% and a yield strength of 163-530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.conditions: 1000 °C, air, 100 hours exposure time, strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1
generation.mechanism: formation of a protective oxide layer
generation.boundary: room-temperature tensile ductility of 8-16%, yield strength of 163-530 MPa at 1000 °C
generation.uncertainty: The actual oxidation rate reduction may vary depending on the specific processing conditions and microstructure of the alloy.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the oxidation rate of the Y-added alloy is not reduced by at least 20% compared to the untreated alloy, or if the room-temperature tensile ductility or yield strength at 1000 °C are reduced by more than 10%, the hypothesis is falsified.
